stem: A written information security policy approved by the board is best described as which control category?

options.why: Policies, risk assessments and security planning are managerial controls: they direct how security is governed.
Directive is a control type, describing what the control does. The question asked for the category. A policy is managerial in category and directive in type.
Operational controls are executed by people day to day, such as awareness training or guard patrols. Writing and approving the policy itself is managerial.
Technical controls are implemented in hardware or software. A document is not.

stem: A nightly backup job is best classified as which control category and type?

options.why: It is implemented in software, and it acts after an incident to restore what was lost.
The category is right and the type is wrong. A backup prevents nothing; it repairs afterwards.
The type is right and the category is wrong. An automated job is technical, not a human process.
Both are wrong. It is not governance, and it does not stand in for a control you could not implement.

stem: A sign at the car park entrance reads 'Warning: this area is under video surveillance.' The sign itself is which control type?

options.why: It discourages an attacker by changing their decision. It physically blocks nothing.
An attacker who ignores the sign is not stopped by it. Nothing is prevented.
The cameras are detective. The sign announcing them is deterrent.
A compensating control substitutes for a control you cannot implement. The sign is not standing in for anything.

stem: Which physical control is preventive rather than deterrent?

options.why: A vehicle physically cannot pass them. The attacker's intent is irrelevant.

options.text: Security lighting in the car park
options.why: Lighting makes an attacker feel exposed, which discourages. It stops nobody who proceeds anyway.

options.text: A visible camera dome in the lobby
options.why: Visible cameras deter, and they detect. They do not prevent entry.

options.text: A sign warning that trespassers will be prosecuted
options.why: Warning signs are the textbook deterrent.

stem: A legacy manufacturing system cannot be patched because the vendor no longer exists and the software will not run on a supported OS. The organisation places it on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs and enhanced monitoring. What kind of control is this?

options.why: The control you wanted, patching, is impossible, so another control is put in place to meet the objective by different means. It is documented as an exception in the risk register.
Corrective controls repair after an incident. Nothing has happened here; this is chosen in advance.
The monitoring component is detective, but the isolation and ACLs are the substance, and the reason for the whole arrangement is substitution.
Directive controls instruct people what to do. This is a technical arrangement.

stem: Which scenario describes a corrective control rather than a compensating one?

options.text: Restoring a database from backup after a failed update corrupted it
options.why: The incident happened and the control repairs the damage. That is corrective.

options.text: Requiring two approvers because the application cannot enforce separation of duties
options.why: The desired control is unavailable, so a different one substitutes for it in advance. That is compensating.

options.text: Adding MFA to a system whose password policy cannot be strengthened
options.why: Again a substitute for a control that cannot be implemented, chosen before anything goes wrong.

options.text: Isolating an unpatchable device on its own network segment
options.why: The classic compensating control for a device that cannot be patched.

stem: Which TWO controls are preventive rather than deterrent? (Choose two.)

options.why: A vehicle physically cannot pass. The attacker's intent is irrelevant, which is what makes it preventive.
It physically stops a second person following the first through the door.

options.text: A sign reading 'These premises are under video surveillance'
options.why: A sign persuades. Anyone who ignores it walks straight past, so it deters and prevents nothing.

options.text: Security lighting across the car park
options.why: Lighting makes an attacker feel exposed. It blocks nobody.
A policy is directive in type and managerial in category. It instructs, it does not prevent.

stem: A SIEM rule raises an alert when the same user authenticates from two countries within an hour. Which control type is the rule?

options.text: Detective: it identifies the event after it has happened and raises it for action
options.why: An alert is the signature output of a detective control. Both logins already succeeded; the rule found out.

options.text: Preventive: the alert stops the second login
options.why: An alert stops nothing. Had the system refused the second login, that refusal would be preventive; raising it afterwards is detective.

options.text: Corrective: it returns the account to a safe state
options.why: Nothing was repaired. Disabling the account or forcing a reset after the alert would be corrective; the rule itself only reports.

options.text: Technical: it is implemented in software
options.why: Technical is the category, and it is correct on that axis. The question asked for the type, which is what the control does about the event.

stem: A badge reader refuses entry to anyone without a valid card, and a camera system records the lobby. Which control types are these, in that order?

options.why: The reader physically stops entry. The recording stops nobody; it gives you evidence afterwards.
The reader does not merely discourage; a determined person without a card is still stopped, which makes it preventive.
A recording prevents nothing. It is reviewed after the event, which is the definition of detective.
Those are categories. The question asks for types.

stem: An organisation updates its acceptable use policy to state that personal cloud storage must not be used for company files, and every employee signs the new version. Which control type is the policy?

options.text: Directive: it instructs staff on the behaviour expected of them
options.why: A policy tells people who intend to comply what to do. That is a directive control, whatever topic it covers.

options.text: Deterrent: it discourages employees from using personal storage
options.why: A deterrent is aimed at someone who intends to do harm and warns them off. The policy is aimed at the compliant and tells them the rule.

options.text: Preventive: with the policy in force, files cannot reach personal storage
options.why: A policy prevents nothing by itself. A DLP rule that blocks the upload would be the preventive control enforcing it.

options.text: Managerial: it is a document approved by management
options.why: Managerial is the right category. The question asked for the type.

stem: Which control is operational rather than managerial or technical?

options.text: Security guards performing hourly patrols of the data centre
options.why: People performing a process on a schedule is the operational category.

options.text: The annual risk assessment approved by the chief information security officer
options.why: A risk assessment is a governing decision document. That is managerial.

options.text: The access control policy requiring multifactor authentication for administrators
options.why: A policy is managerial. It governs; it does not carry anything out.

options.text: The multifactor authentication system enforcing the second factor
options.why: A system enforcing with no person in the loop is technical.

stem: A payment application is required to log every administrative action, but the vendor's software cannot write audit logs. The team places a network tap and records every administrative session to the application instead. Which control type is the session recording?

options.text: Compensating: it stands in for the audit logging the application cannot provide
options.why: The stem says the required control could not be implemented and this one was put in its place. That makes it compensating, whatever its own mechanism.

options.text: Detective: a recording identifies what happened after the fact
options.why: By mechanism it does detect, but the exam classifies a substitute for a required control as compensating. The stem spelled out the substitution.

options.text: Corrective: it fixes the application's missing capability
options.why: Nothing was repaired and no incident happened. A control chosen in advance because the wanted one is impossible is compensating.

options.text: Physical: a tap is a piece of hardware
options.why: That is a category argument, and a weak one; the question asks for the type.

stem: Which TWO are detective controls? (Choose two.)

options.text: An analyst reviewing firewall logs every morning
options.why: Reviewing logs finds out what happened. It stops nothing and fixes nothing, which is exactly detective.

options.text: An intrusion detection system on a network tap
options.why: An IDS watches a copy of the traffic and raises an alert. Detection is in the name.

options.text: A warning sign at the perimeter fence
options.why: A sign notices nothing. It discourages, which is deterrent.
Encryption prevents disclosure. It reports nothing, so it cannot be detective.

stem: Which control is deterrent rather than directive?

options.text: A sign stating that the premises are patrolled by guard dogs
options.why: It is aimed at someone considering an intrusion and warns them off. That is a deterrent.

options.text: A sign instructing visitors to sign in at reception
options.why: That sign gives an instruction to people who intend to comply. It is directive.
Training tells people how to behave. Directive.
A policy instructs. It threatens nobody, so it is directive, not deterrent.

stem: A company documents a procedure for provisioning new starters, and the help desk follows it every Monday morning. Which categories do the written procedure and the weekly execution belong to?

options.why: The document governs how the work is done, which is managerial. People carrying it out is operational.
The procedure document carries nothing out. A written control that governs is managerial; only its execution is operational.
A procedure is not a system enforcing anything. Technical controls act without a person in the loop.
The help desk performing the steps is people doing a process. That is operational, not a management decision.
